articles.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
articles.titleZh: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
articles.summary: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months

blocks.text: 24th November 2026

I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.
Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.
Coding agents in November 2025
Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.
In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.
This held up.
Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant.
The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.
Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.
After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st.
For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.
Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.
These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.
3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here’s Gemini 4 Neon’s attempt at “Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data”, for example.
3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don’t know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 “This game isn’t fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.” And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I’d used that appeared to understand fun. I’ve since worked on several little game projects where prompts like “Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful” produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I’ve been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they’d been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.
The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.
It feels like another inflection point to me.
Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?
I’m still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.
I’m getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I’ve been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44—plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38—all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That’s a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.
Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don’t think I’ll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

articles.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
articles.titleZh: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
articles.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

blocks.text: 24th November 2026 - Link Blog
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery. Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.
Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.
Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

articles.title: Engadget Scoop Claims iPhone 18e Will Have a Camera Plateau
articles.titleZh: Engadget Scoop Claims iPhone 18e Will Have a Camera Plateau
articles.summary: Engadget Scoop Claims iPhone 18e Will Have a Camera Plateau

blocks.text: We've also got further confirmation the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera.
Diego Thomazini/Getty Images

Apple seems to have adopted a new strategy for the iPhone launch, splitting it into two phases. After launching the premium iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo in September, Apple is preparing new versions of the lower-priced models — and it looks like they'll look a lot more like the more expensive iPhones. CAD images of the new iPhone 18e seen by Engadget show a redesigned camera bump on the back of the phone, similar to the one on the Pro models. The images come from a source familiar with Apple's supply chain who who had previously shared accurate tips on the colors of the iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro before they were announced.

The current iPhone 17e doesn't have a camera bump — instead, the lens has a small protrusion and sits flush against the back of the phone, with the microphone and LED flash also embedded in cutouts directly in the rear glass. But according to CAD images seen by Engadget, Apple appears to be considering changing that with the iPhone 18e. The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone. It's somewhat similar to the camera module on the M5 iPad Pro (which you can see in the image below).

Interestingly, it seems that the iPhone 18e will be the only model to feature this new camera plateau. The same files include the CADs for the base iPhone 18 and the iPhone Air 2, both of which are expected to launch alongside the 18e next spring. The base iPhone 18 will keep the exact same design, but now with a thicker camera module — increasing from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches). Apple has been using the same 48-megapixel Sony IMX904 sensor for its base models since the iPhone 15, so a thicker camera module could mean new sensors or upgraded cameras.

As for the iPhone Air 2, the CADs seen by Engadget corroborate previous rumors that Apple's ultra-thin phone will feature a second rear camera — not a surprise given that its single lens was one of the main complaints about it. Although the Air 2 will remain 5.6mm thick, the camera module will increase in thickness from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches), with the two lenses aligned horizontally. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the leaker Digital Chat Station and analyst Jeff Pu have all said Apple is adding an ultra-wide lens to the second-generation Air, and the CAD images back those reports up.

Also, the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are expected to keep the same Dynamic Island as current models rather than the smaller cutout on the iPhone 18 Pro. Of course, these changes may end up being scrapped and never see the light of day, since Apple still has some time before they hit the stores next year.

articles.title: Trump Made Up to $15M on Nvidia Stock After Huang’s Return
articles.titleZh: Trump Made Up to $15M on Nvidia Stock After Huang’s Return
articles.summary: Trump Made Up to $15M on Nvidia Stock After Huang’s Return

blocks.text: Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from the US president.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them  … I made the deal.”

The US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times.

Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% on Monday, adding about $950bn to the company’s value. Huang returned to the company’s HQ in Santa Clara, California, receiving a hero’s welcome, with crowds of employees chanting “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”

Trump has bought Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m, according to a BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the past two years. He has also sold some of his stake in the company since returning to the presidency, and gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
Huang’s surprising, and controversial, return to run Nvidia – which is at the heart of the global AI boom – prompted a strong rally in Asia-Pacific stock markets on Tuesday.

Stocks soared in Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, and Australia, as the AI trade lurched back into life after a tumultuous few months. Taiwan’s TW50 index leapt by 9.5%, while South Korea’s Kospi index jumped by 6.5%, led by the chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Japan’s Nikkei gained almost 4%. Stock markets across Europe were broadly flat.

In the US, stock markets opened down, with the S&P 500 off 0.4% and the tech- heavy Nasdaq down 1.8%. Nvidia’s shares fell 6% in early trading. Anthropic, the AI company which sold shares in its record-breaking flotation last week, saw its stock drop by 8.3% at the start of trading, to $80.34, below the $83 IPO price.
after newsletter promotion

That followed a rise on Wall Street on Monday. AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months, amid worries over high debt levels in the sector to fund the AI infrastructure buildout, as well as the prospect of tougher regulation in the US after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

Ruben Gallego, a Democrat senator from Arizona, posted on X: “We need to investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement. This White House is the most corrupt in history.” He later posted: “Trump may have started the popping of the AI bubble.”

Roger Lee, the head of equity strategy at the investment bank Cavendish, said: “Given Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the [global financial crisis], are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired?

“Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally.”
Economists said Huang’s return meant the US Federal Reserve was more likely to raise interest rates, with the prospect of the AI bubble bursting imminently diminishing.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said: “With fears of an AI slowdown receding, it also led markets to price back in a more hawkish path for the Federal Reserve over the months ahead.
“So for the next meeting in December, markets are once again fully pricing in a 25 basis point hike.”

WASHINGTON — President Trump claimed Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could have become a leader in China’s artificial intelligence industry if he hadn’t been reinstated to the US firm — telling CNBC in a phone interview that the 63-year-old has “got a little blood there” despite being born in Taiwan.

“If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ’Hey, how would you like to come to China?’ — He’s got a little [Chinese] blood in him. He’s got a little blood there — ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei?’” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview, during which he called Huang, 63, a “national treasure” despite his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that.”

Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to restore the AI pioneer 11 days after he resigned — saying he gave the directors assurances that Huang wouldn’t face legal issues over his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation).
If Alice Huang or her Singapore-based Megaspeed firm violated US export laws by sending advanced Nvidia chips to China, “that wouldn’t be Jensen’s fault,” Trump argued.

The president, who returned late Thursday from a trip to China that included a trilateral summit with his counterpart Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, reiterated that “Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you they would give him whatever he wanted.
“And then they’d automatically have you know all of the things. He never even suggested that. But I know how good China is, how professional they are, how cunning they are.”

Trump said during his nearly hour-long interview that he didn’t ask Xi if Alice Huang was a spy — a claim Beijing has denied though Megaspeed was under investigation by Singapore’s government and the US Commerce Department for allegedly flouting US export restrictions on AI chip shipping to China.

“You know, he’s in a class by himself. We would have lost him,” Trump said of Huang, who was sent to the US by his parents at age 9, cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into one of the world’s most valuable companies.
“If I were President Xi, I’d say, ‘Hey, let’s get him over here real fast. He can have whatever he wants. We’ll give him Beijing. Okay, we’ll give him all of Beijing.’”
“Crazy things like that happen,” Trump said.
“I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level. He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate…. That’s what brought it to such a level because sex sells, fellas.”
